scenes.visual: Dark slate background. Title 'Reading a Signal in Time' centred in crisp white (size 48). Behind it, two horizontal guide tracks begin drawing left to right: an amber signal track on top and a teal decoder track below, establishing the colour map used throughout both films (amber = signal, teal = decoder, bright green = active/stabilized output, coral = decay/brake).

scenes.tts: Two growth factors switch on the exact same kinase, E R K, inside one cell. Why does one order division while the other orders nerve-like branches? If the molecule is identical, something else in the signal must carry the difference.
scenes.caption: Two growth factors switch on the exact same kinase, ERK, inside one cell. Why does one order division while the other orders nerve-like branches? If the molecule is identical, something else in the signal must carry the difference.
scenes.visual: Full-frame schematic of a rat PC12 cell split down the middle. Left half: amber badge 'EGF' triggers amber 'ERK' glow and the cell smoothly splits in two ('Divide'). Right half: amber badge 'NGF' triggers the exact same amber 'ERK' glow and the cell extends long thin branches ('Differentiate'). A pulsing amber question mark sits between the two identical ERK blocks. Label 'schematic' small in corner.
scenes.narration: Two growth factors switch on the exact same kinase, ERK, inside one cell. Why does one order division while the other orders nerve-like branches? If the molecule is identical, something else in the signal must carry the difference.

scenes.tts: Cells reuse a small toolkit of messengers, so identity is only part of the message. A cell also reads four features: how much, how long, how often, and where. Reading time takes a decoder, a downstream protein with its own built-in speed.
scenes.caption: Cells reuse a small toolkit of messengers, so identity is only part of the message. A cell also reads four features: how much, how long, how often, and where. Reading time takes a decoder, a downstream protein with its own built-in speed.
scenes.visual: The cell morphs into the film's carried world: a large two-lane timeline filling 70% of the frame. Four crisp amber icons sweep across the top lane as spoken: tall vs short bar ('How much'), brief vs long plateau ('How long'), slow vs rapid spikes ('How often'), and a localized dot ('Where'). Then the bottom teal lane lights up with a 'Decoder' block and a steadily ticking clock icon beside it.
scenes.narration: Cells reuse a small toolkit of messengers, so identity is only part of the message. A cell also reads four features: how much, how long, how often, and where. Reading time takes a decoder, a downstream protein with its own built-in speed.

scenes.tts: Start with how long. E G F turns E R K on briefly, while N G F keeps E R K on much longer. A cell has no stopwatch. Instead, it compares E R K against a delayed protein that the same signal switches on.
scenes.caption: Start with how long. EGF turns ERK on briefly, while NGF keeps ERK on much longer. A cell has no stopwatch. Instead, it compares ERK against a delayed protein that the same signal switches on.
scenes.visual: Carried two-lane timeline (labelled 'schematic'). Top amber lane plots two overlaid ERK activity curves: a short pulse ('EGF: brief ERK') and a long plateau ('NGF: long ERK'). A dashed vertical clock line sweeps rightward while a teal arrow drops from the amber ERK track down into the bottom lane, labelled 'Delayed product'.
scenes.narration: Start with how long. EGF turns ERK on briefly, while NGF keeps ERK on much longer. A cell has no stopwatch. Instead, it compares ERK against a delayed protein that the same signal switches on.

scenes.tts: In fibroblasts, E R K switches on a gene called C fos. Building C fos protein takes time, and fresh C fos breaks down quickly. Rapid destruction sounds wasteful, yet it works as a timer. Only if E R K stays on until C fos appears can phosphates protect it.
scenes.caption: In fibroblasts, ERK switches on a gene called c-fos. Building c-Fos protein takes time, and fresh c-Fos breaks down quickly. Rapid destruction sounds wasteful, yet it works as a timer. Only if ERK stays on until c-Fos appears can phosphates protect it.
scenes.visual: Carried two-lane timeline stays in place (labelled 'schematic'). Two routes connect top amber ERK to bottom teal c-Fos: a slow winding path ('Slow route: make c-Fos') and a direct vertical arrow ('Fast route: add phosphates'). Left run (brief ERK): ERK drops to zero before teal c-Fos arrives; coral fragments show fresh c-Fos breaking down. Right run (long ERK): amber ERK is still high when c-Fos arrives; phosphate badges snap on, turning c-Fos bright green and rising smoothly.
scenes.narration: In fibroblasts, ERK switches on a gene called c-fos. Building c-Fos protein takes time, and fresh c-Fos breaks down quickly. Rapid destruction sounds wasteful, yet it works as a timer. Only if ERK stays on until c-Fos appears can phosphates protect it.

scenes.tts: Pause and test this timer. Suppose a mutation makes fresh C fos stable right away, with no phosphates needed. After a brief E G F pulse, will C fos now build up, or still vanish?
scenes.caption: Pause and test this timer. Suppose a mutation makes fresh c-Fos stable right away, with no phosphates needed. After a brief EGF pulse, will c-Fos now build up, or still vanish?
scenes.visual: Top amber lane shows the brief EGF pulse rising and dropping back to zero. Bottom lane shows emerging teal c-Fos blocks wearing a shield icon ('Always stable — mutant'). Bold white question banner at top: 'Brief ERK + always-stable c-Fos: build up, or vanish?' Two dashed preview curves shimmer gently in the bottom lane: one rising in bright green, one fading in coral.
scenes.narration: Pause and test this timer. Suppose a mutation makes fresh c-Fos stable right away, with no phosphates needed. After a brief EGF pulse, will c-Fos now build up, or still vanish?

scenes.visual: Hold the question banner 'Brief ERK + always-stable c-Fos: build up, or vanish?' with the brief amber ERK pulse and the two gently shimmering preview curves (rising green vs fading coral). A subtle white countdown ring ticks smoothly for 4.5 seconds so the frame stays alive.

scenes.tts: It builds up, because without fast breakdown, C fos survives even after E R K shuts off. Brief and long signals now look alike, so the decoder has lost its clock. Now carry that idea to repeating spikes.
scenes.caption: It builds up, because without fast breakdown, c-Fos survives even after ERK shuts off. Brief and long signals now look alike, so the decoder has lost its clock. Now carry that idea to repeating spikes.
scenes.visual: The rising bright-green curve locks in solidly on the bottom lane while the fading coral curve disappears. Label 'Clock broken: brief looks like long' flashes cleanly, then clears. The top amber lane smoothly morphs from a plateau into a train of sharp vertical calcium spikes, carrying the exact same two-lane timeline into frequency decoding.
scenes.narration: It builds up, because without fast breakdown, c-Fos survives even after ERK shuts off. Brief and long signals now look alike, so the decoder has lost its clock. Now carry that idea to repeating spikes.

scenes.tts: Calcium often rises in brief spikes of similar height, and in many cells stronger cues send faster spikes. A cell counts them using a decoder that turns on fast and decays slowly. Picture a leaky bucket: rare cups drain away, while rapid cups stack higher. Each spike adds onto whatever activity remains.
scenes.caption: Calcium often rises in brief spikes of similar height, and in many cells stronger cues send faster spikes. A cell counts them using a decoder that turns on fast and decays slowly. Picture a leaky bucket: rare cups drain away, while rapid cups stack higher. Each spike adds onto whatever activity remains.
scenes.visual: Carried two-lane timeline plus a compact teal leaky-bucket inset on the left with coral drops dripping from a small hole. Each amber calcium spike in the top lane pours a bright-green cup into the bucket and jumps the bottom-lane decoder trace upward. Between spikes, the bucket drips coral droplets and the teal curve decays smoothly.
scenes.narration: Calcium often rises in brief spikes of similar height, and in many cells stronger cues send faster spikes. A cell counts them using a decoder that turns on fast and decays slowly. Picture a leaky bucket: rare cups drain away, while rapid cups stack higher. Each spike adds onto whatever activity remains.

scenes.tts: The fraction left equals one half to the power of gap divided by half-time. Take a thirty-second half-time. With spikes one hundred twenty seconds apart, one twenty divided by thirty is four half-times. One half four times leaves one sixteenth, about six percent. At fifteen seconds apart, fifteen divided by thirty is half a half-time. One half to the power of one half leaves about seventy-one percent.
scenes.caption: The fraction left equals (1/2)^(gap ÷ half-time). Take a 30-second half-time. With spikes 120 s apart, 120 ÷ 30 = 4 half-times. (1/2)^4 leaves 1/16, about 6%. At 15 s apart, 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5 half-times. (1/2)^0.5 leaves about 71%.
scenes.visual: Exact computed exponential-decay curves from y(t) = 2^(-t/30) fill the carried two-lane timeline (computed, not schematic). Formula appears at top in crisp white (size 30): 'fraction left = (1/2)^(gap ÷ half-time)', with 'half-time = 30 s' in teal. Left half animates amber spikes every 120 s: labels appear synchronously as spoken: '120 ÷ 30 = 4', '(1/2)^4 = 1/16 ≈ 6%', and the teal curve drains nearly flat before each spike. Right half animates amber spikes every 15 s: '15 ÷ 30 = 0.5', '(1/2)^0.5 ≈ 71%', and the bright-green staircase climbs sharply.
scenes.narration: The fraction left equals (1/2)^(gap ÷ half-time). Take a 30-second half-time. With spikes 120 s apart, 120 ÷ 30 = 4 half-times. (1/2)^4 leaves 1/16, about 6%. At 15 s apart, 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5 half-times. (1/2)^0.5 leaves about 71%.

scenes.tts: Duration and frequency follow one rule. Compare a signal against a decoder's delay or decay, and one messenger carries many orders. Next, read how real proteins do this, and meet one hormone that needs the gaps.

A glowing teal clock icon links both sides gently pulsing, then fades smoothly to dark slate.
